title: Gap analysis and review of survey effort disruption in North Sea and North-eastern Atlantic bottom trawl surveys
content:
Abstract
Fisheries-independent surveys are essential to stock assessment, providing estimates on relative abundance, distribution, and biology of commercially fished species. Environmental, mechanical, and logistical issues can disrupt survey operation and reduce survey effort. We synthesized causes of disruptions to surveys using 25 years of publicly available records for North Sea and North-eastern Atlantic bottom trawl survey operations. We assigned each recorded disruption one of three categories: Spatial—long-term (e.g. windfarms, marine protected areas), Spatial—short-term (e.g. fisheries, mechanical, and legal issues), and random spatial processes (e.g. weather and mechanical issues). Furthermore, we analysed spatiotemporal patterns of survey effort relative to effort targets identified in the survey protocols for bottom trawl surveys in the North Sea and the North-East Atlantic. Lastly, we conducted a case study on the Irish survey (IGFS) to explore the effect of weather, time, and geographic position on the probability of sampling an IGFS station using a binomial generalized additive model. On average, the number of stations sampled was lower than the targets indicated in the sampling protocol for the North Sea and Irish surveys. Weather had consistent effects on effort in all three surveys, implying that their designs are vulnerable to the influence of environmental factors. However, neither storminess (using wave height as a proxy) nor station location was a reliable predictor of sampling probability in the IGFS survey. We provide a framework for analysing the robustness of survey designs to disruption. Our approach could be used in the future to monitor changes in survey effort in relation to protocols, facilitating critical evaluation of survey design efficacy.
